column2: I check for a Global.cs file that says public class Global and holds all fourteen public static lines.
This part adds one new file to your project. It is called Global.cs.
I meet the words Global, variable and static before I use them.
A form forgets everything when it closes, so Global.cs keeps what every form needs.
I add a class called Global and put the word public in front of class.
This part types fourteen lines into Global.cs. Each line keeps one thing about the pupil.
Global.cs holds four string variables for the surname, first name, year group and gender, each starting empty.
Global.cs holds three int attempts, a double average and a bool that says if the average is worked out.
Global.cs holds the quiz score, the reaction test score, a bool for each saying it is taken, and the group.
The project builds, and typing Global and a full stop in another form lists all fourteen names.
I check that the Enter button has code, starts with string errors, lists what is missing, and switches the panels.
This part gives the Enter button four checks. Each one adds a line to a list called errors.
I open the code behind the Enter button and meet the six new things in this chapter.
The Enter button starts with an empty string called errors, so every problem found can be added to it.
If the surname box or the first name box is empty, a line saying so is added to errors.
A name over 20 letters adds a too long line, and an empty drop-down list adds a must select line.
This part shows every problem in one message. With no problems, it keeps the details and switches panels.
If errors has anything in it, one message box shows every problem found.
With no problems, the surname, first name, gender and year group each go into their line in Global.cs.
I watch the details panel switch off and the attempts panel switch on.
After the details are kept, the attempts panel switches on and the details panel switches off.
I run the program and try empty boxes, a long surname, all four filled in, and typing in the grey panel.
I check the average button has code, refuses letters, and shows 6 for 5, 6 and 7.
This part gives the average button three checks. A bool called passValidation remembers if any check failed.
I open the code behind the average button and meet the six new things in this chapter.
The average button starts with a bool called passValidation set to true. Any failed check turns it false.
If any of the three attempt boxes is empty, passValidation is set to false.
If the first attempt box holds something that is not a number from 0 to 9, passValidation is set to false.
The same letter check is done for the second and third attempt boxes.
If passValidation is false, a message asks for numbers only and the three boxes are emptied.
This part adds the three attempts and divides by 3. It keeps the answer in Global.cs.
The three attempts are added, divided by 3, rounded to 2 places, kept in Global.cs and shown in the box.
Global.cs notes the average is worked out and keeps the three attempts. The attempts panel switches off.
I watch the attempts panel switch off and the quiz panel switch on.
After the attempts are kept, the quiz panel switches on so the pupil can move on.
I run the program and try letters, 5 6 7, 5 6 8, and typing in the grey attempts panel.
